lessonRef.title: Performance task build: editing to a style manual

studentTask.text: This English 9 lesson develops editing to a style manual within the unit “Named Grammatical Structures and Style-Manual Conformance.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's performance task build work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
[1] In the “Named Grammatical Structures and Style-Manual Conformance” workshop at the public radio studio, Samir compared an early draft beside the writer's published version. The early version said, “The committee quickly approved the surprisingly modest plan.” The revision said, “After twelve minutes of questions, the committee approved the plan by a four-to-three vote.”

[2] The first sentence was shorter, but its adverbs quietly told the reader how to judge speed and scale. The second replaced those judgments with measurable details. It sounded less certain about what counted as quick or modest, yet it gave the reader more material for an independent conclusion.

[3] Amara then changed the verb “approved” to “accepted.” The facts did not change, but the tone did. “Approved” suggested endorsement; “accepted” could suggest reluctant agreement. Neither verb was always correct. The surrounding purpose and evidence had to decide which shade of meaning fit.

[4] To study editing to a style manual, the workshop tracked how syntax, punctuation, and word choice accumulated across the passage. One change altered emphasis; several coordinated changes altered the writer's stance. The strongest edit was not automatically the most formal one, but the one whose effect matched a clearly named purpose.

[5] Before revising, the group tested the source against the workshop goal: editing to a style manual. They highlighted language that supported the goal, circled a detail that complicated it, and drew an arrow where the relationship between two ideas needed to be made explicit. The marks produced different possible readings, so the group had to defend priorities rather than copy a single approved answer.

[6] A later reader complicated the discussion by asking about audience and purpose. A concise public notice, a literary interpretation, and a research explanation may use evidence differently even when all three are responsible. The group therefore recorded not only what the source said, but also what situation would make each interpretation effective, insufficient, or misleading.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “Reading Lab 138: editing to a style manual”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what editing to a style manual asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “Reading Lab 138: editing to a style manual,” then answer: Draft the planned response about editing to a style manual. How will each paragraph use the reading rather than merely mention it?

Deliverable: English 9: a complete first draft with source-based development in every body section; write a structured response of 500–700 words.

Evidence requirement: Use two precise quotations or paraphrases with paragraph numbers. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If editing to a style manual is not yet secure, return to “Reading Lab 138: editing to a style manual” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply editing to a style manual to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “Reading Lab 138: editing to a style manual.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
